title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
elicitation_reason: Runs zero experiments: each of the five failure modes is named, illustrated with a fictional cleaning robot, and closed with a proposed-but-unexecuted experiment. Nothing is produced from a model at all, so the paper licenses vocabulary, not rates.
eval_awareness_reason: No model is measured anywhere in the paper, and the 2016 framing is classic RL agents that cannot represent being evaluated.
locus_reason: Four of the five problems (negative side effects, reward hacking, safe exploration, distributional-shift robustness) are properties of the objective and its optimization; only scalable oversight sits outside the training loop, in the human feedback channel.
detectability_reason: Reward hacking and negative side effects are by construction invisible from the reward signal you have — you need the designer's true objective, which the paper's whole premise is that you do not have.
mitigation_status_reason: Every section ends with a proposed research direction and experiment; none is executed or evaluated in the paper.
harm_bearer_reason: The framing is 'accidents' — the deploying principal's own goal is subverted by the system it built; third-party harm (the cleaning robot knocking over a vase) is the illustration, not the analytic frame.
placement_reason: The founding attempt to carve AI failure into engineering-tractable classes organized around where the ML pipeline breaks — wrong objective, unaffordable oversight, bad learning-time decisions — and the ancestor every later reward-hacking and oversight taxonomy cites.
one_line: Names five near-term ML accident failure modes — negative side effects, reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, distributional-shift robustness — with zero experiments; 3,292 citations of vocabulary rather than evidence.
key_number: 5 failure modes, 0 experiments, 3,292 citations
notes: Explicitly brackets privacy, fairness, security, abuse, transparency and policy as out of scope. The eval read notes the taxonomy aged unevenly: reward hacking and scalable oversight became load-bearing, safe exploration far less so.

title: Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law
elicitation_reason: A conceptual/formal taxonomy paper: every one of the eight mechanisms is illustrated with a hand-built statistical or causal toy model (M = G + noise, wind sensors, cobra bounties), never with a system exhibiting the failure.
eval_awareness_reason: No model, no measurement — the regulator/proxy formalism is agent-agnostic.
locus_reason: The whole formalism is about a selector restricting states to {s : M(s) >= c} using a proxy metric — i.e. the optimization pressure applied against a training/selection signal.
evidence_mode_reason: Derivation-based rather than empirical: regressional Goodhart falls out of a noise model, causal Goodhart out of an intervention model. Coded formal-proof for the mode of argument, but the derivations are single-dimensional toy models, not general theorems — the paper concedes the categories overlap and never separates them on real data.
detectability_reason: Every category is defined by divergence between the proxy M and the unobserved goal G; without G you cannot tell which Goodhart variant (or any) is occurring — the paper's own unanswered operational question.
harm_bearer_reason: The victim in the formalism is the regulator/principal whose true goal G silently stops being served.
placement_reason: The formal skeleton later reward-hacking work builds on: it turns 'optimizing a proxy breaks it' into four distinguishable mechanisms with different causes, which is the vocabulary Gao 2022 and Skalse 2022 adopt directly.
one_line: Splits Goodhart's Law into regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial mechanisms (eight sub-mechanisms including the Cobra Effect), all derived on toy models with zero empirical cases.
key_number: 4 base categories / 8 sub-mechanisms, 0 empirical validations
notes: Formal treatment restricted to the single-dimensional case; the paper explicitly concedes category overlap, so 'which Goodhart type is this?' is not an operational diagnostic.

title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
elicitation_reason: Ordinary XSum documents, ordinary summarization decoding, no adversary and no engineered input: hallucination is the default output mode, present in 73-79% of summaries including the human-written references.
eval_awareness_reason: 2020 seq2seq summarizers (PTGEN, TConvS2S, TranS2S, BERTS2S) have no capacity to condition behaviour on believing they are under evaluation.
locus_reason: The source document is in context and is correct; the deviation comes from the model's own generative prior overriding it, which is why pretrained-init BERTS2S hallucinates differently from the copy-mechanism PTGEN.
evidence_mode_reason: 2,500 human faithfulness judgments across five systems, reported as per-system rates with an intrinsic/extrinsic split.
detectability_reason: The summary reads fluently and scores well; you must hold it against the source article to see the unsupported span, and the paper shows ROUGE/BERTScore cannot do that (|rs| ~ 0.16-0.20).
mitigation_status_reason: Two partial levers are demonstrated, neither a fix: pretrained initialization lowers hallucination somewhat (BERTS2S 73.1% vs TranS2S 79.3%), and an entailment classifier tracks faithfulness better than overlap metrics (0.431/0.264 vs 0.16-0.20) — but that is improved detection, and 73% still hallucinate.
harm_bearer_reason: The reader of a fluent, confidently wrong one-sentence summary is the party misled.
placement_reason: The founding large-scale measurement of unfaithfulness to a provided source, and the origin of the intrinsic/extrinsic vocabulary that every later grounded-generation faithfulness paper inherits.
one_line: 73-79% of single-sentence XSum summaries contain content the source never supports — including 76.9% of the human-written GOLD references — while ROUGE/BERTScore barely correlate with faithfulness (|rs| ~ 0.16-0.20).
key_number: 73-79% of summaries hallucinated; GOLD references 76.9%; ROUGE-faithfulness Spearman ~ 0.16-0.20
notes: The GOLD-reference hallucination rate is the sharpest result: the reference standard itself is unfaithful, so training data teaches the behaviour.

title: Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
elicitation_reason: No adversary and no crafted attack — the failure appears in the most ordinary use of the model there was in 2021 (pick four labelled examples, put them in a prompt). It only requires a sweep to *see*, not to *produce*.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-2/GPT-3 base models scored by output-token likelihood; there is no mechanism by which believing itself evaluated could change the measured accuracy.
locus_reason: The failure is caused by what is in the prompt and in what order — majority-label, recency and common-token biases are shifts in the output distribution induced by the context, not by the task.
evidence_mode_reason: The design is a permutation A/B: identical examples, identical template, order varied — which is what isolates order as the cause rather than example quality.
detectability_reason: A single run gives one number that looks fine; you only see the failure by re-running with a permuted prompt, which almost no reported few-shot result does.
mitigation_status_reason: Contextual calibration adds up to +30.0 points absolute and shrinks variance in most cells, but the paper's own Table 1 shows it re-centres rather than removes the sensitivity — the underlying representation of (examples, order, format) is untouched.
harm_bearer_reason: The immediate casualty is the reported number: a single-seed few-shot score can be tens of points off what a different ordering would give, so leaderboard entries of the era measured prompt luck as much as capability.
placement_reason: The first precise diagnosis that a headline few-shot capability number is dominated by prompt configuration rather than model capability, with a named mechanism (three output-distribution biases) rather than a shrug.
one_line: Reordering the same four SST-2 examples swings GPT-3 2.7B from 54.3% to 93.4% accuracy; a content-free 'N/A' probe recovers up to +30.0 points but narrows rather than removes the spread.
key_number: 54.3% -> 93.4% from example order alone; up to +30.0 points absolute from contextual calibration
notes: Calibrated GPT-3 2.7B sometimes beats the uncalibrated 175B by up to 19.3 points — a 50x-smaller model, which is the sharpest statement of how much of a reported score was prompt artifact.

title: Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity
elicitation_reason: Same ordinary few-shot usage as Zhao et al.; the permutation sweep is the measurement apparatus, not an attack.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-2/GPT-3-family base models on text classification; no eval-context mechanism exists.
evidence_mode_reason: Examples and template held fixed, only order varied across 24 permutations x 8 model sizes — the cleanest available isolation of order as the cause.
detectability_reason: Nothing in a single ordering's output signals that it is a bad ordering; the paper explicitly finds 'no common denominator between performant sample orders' and no transfer across model sizes (rho as low as 0.05).
mitigation_status_reason: Entropy-based ordering selection buys an average 13% (up to 30%) relative gain with zero labelled data, but the label-using Oracle still beats it (88.9+/-1.8 vs 84.8+/-4.1 on GPT-2 0.8B/SST-2), so headroom the statistic cannot reach remains.
harm_bearer_reason: Like Zhao et al., the party harmed is anyone reading a single-configuration few-shot number as a capability estimate.
placement_reason: Isolates order alone (not selection or format) as sufficient to move accuracy from near-chance to near-SOTA, and shows the good orderings are model-specific and unpredictable — the strongest form of the prompt-fragility result.
one_line: Holding examples and template fixed and varying only order swings GPT-family accuracy from near-chance to SOTA (a single ordering fell 88.7% -> 51.6% just from GPT2-XL to GPT2-Large), and entropy-ranked orderings recover an average 13% relative.
key_number: average 13% (up to 30%) relative gain from ordering selection; cross-model-size ordering correlation as low as rho = 0.05
notes: Deliberately agnostic about mechanism, unlike Zhao's three named biases — its lever is search over orderings, not correction of logits.

title: Understanding Factuality in Abstractive Summarization with FRANK: A Benchmark for Factuality Metrics
elicitation_reason: Ordinary CNN/DM and XSum summarization outputs from nine systems; the paper's work is annotation, not elicitation.
eval_awareness_reason: 2021 summarization systems plus automatic metrics; the subject of measurement is partly the metrics themselves, which cannot be eval-aware.
locus_reason: Two failures are reported and they sit in different places: models make factual errors (weights-prior), but the paper's headline subject is that the automatic factuality *metrics* fail to track human judgment (best partial Pearson 0.27). Coded by the headline subject; the model-error catalogue is the substrate.
evidence_mode_reason: 2,250 human-annotated summaries with three annotators per sentence, then partial correlations of each metric against those labels.
detectability_reason: The paper's whole result is that no cheap automatic proxy substitutes for a human reading the summary against the source.
mitigation_status_reason: Diagnostic by design: it supplies a typology and a meta-evaluation protocol, not a fix for either the models' factual errors or the metrics' weakness.
harm_bearer_reason: The damage is to the field's ability to certify factuality automatically — every metric benchmarked here was being used as if it could.
placement_reason: A benchmark whose subject is factuality metrics rather than models: it replaces the binary factual/non-factual label with a seven-category typology and scores the metrics against it, which is meta-evaluation of the instrument.
one_line: 60.0% of 2,250 annotated summaries contain at least one factual error (XSum's best model wrong 83.7% of the time), and the best automatic metric reaches only partial Pearson 0.27 against human judgment.
key_number: 60.0% of summaries carry a factual error; best metric partial Pearson 0.27 (FactCC 0.20)
notes: Version-sensitive: the bug-fixed arXiv v2 gives BERTScore-P 0.27 where the published NAACL PDF still shows an insignificant -0.02. Full-dataset agreement is modest (kappa 0.58 binary, 0.39 for the 8-category split); the headline kappa 0.86 is a 201-datapoint spot-check.

title: Goal Misgeneralization in Deep Reinforcement Learning
elicitation_reason: The failure is manufactured by the training distribution — agents trained on CoinRun levels where the coin is always at the end learn 'move right'. Genuinely ambiguous between trained-in and constructed-scenario, since it takes both a correlated training signal and a deliberately shifted test level to see; coded trained-in because the training distribution is the causal ingredient (2% randomized levels largely removes it) and the test shift only reveals it.
eval_awareness_reason: Procgen RL policies with no language interface and no representation of being evaluated.
locus_reason: The strongest evidence is internal, not behavioural: the critic's value function itself misgeneralizes (coin presence has 'an insignificant effect' on value), so the wrong goal is baked into the learned parameters.
evidence_mode_reason: The randomized-coin sweep separates 'Failure of Capability' from 'Goal Misgeneralization' as distinct measured curves, plus a visible-coin baseline policy as control.
detectability_reason: On the training distribution the agent is indistinguishable from a correct one; you must move the coin to see that it never wanted the coin.
mitigation_status_reason: Randomizing the coin in just 2% of training levels 'greatly improves' goal generalization, but the mitigation is only demonstrated in CoinRun and presupposes you already guessed which correlation to break.
harm_bearer_reason: The principal who specified the reward gets a competent agent pursuing a different objective.
placement_reason: The canonical demonstration that capability and goal generalize separately — the agent keeps every skill out of distribution and applies them to the wrong target — which is a distinct mechanism from reward misspecification (the reward here is correct).
one_line: A CoinRun agent still dodges every obstacle when the coin is moved — it just walks past it; goal misgeneralization is high when no training level randomizes the coin and falls off sharply once 2% do.
key_number: goal misgeneralization collapses once 2% of training levels randomize the coin; agent/device test separates goal from capability at 0.9999 vs 0.0674
notes: The formal capability-retention test (0.9999 vs 0.0674) is computed on a bespoke 20x20 gridworld, never on CoinRun/Maze/Keys-and-Chests, so the headline demos rest on qualitative capability-retention claims. Circulated for ~13 months as 'Objective Robustness' before adopting Shah et al.'s term.

title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
elicitation_reason: 817 questions hand-written specifically so the most likely human answer is false, 437 of them adversarially filtered against GPT-3-175B. The falsehoods do not appear in ordinary questions — the control set of matched trivia scales normally — so a deliberately written probe is required.
eval_awareness_reason: The 2021 base models tested were unlikely to condition on being evaluated, but the questions have a distinctive quiz register and TruthfulQA is still run on eval-aware frontier models today; the paper never checks, so the modern reading of the number is unguarded.
locus_reason: Imitative falsehood is a property of what the pretraining distribution taught: the model reproduces common human misconceptions, which is why the effect grows with scale.
evidence_mode_reason: The matched-control trivia set is what makes the inverse-scaling claim credible — truthfulness falls with size on TruthfulQA while rising with size on controls, isolating imitation rather than general incompetence.
detectability_reason: False-and-informative answers (42% of the best model's replies vs 6% for the human) read as confident and plausible; only a labelled reference reveals them.
mitigation_status_reason: The paper argues fine-tuning/RLHF rather than scale is the route to truthfulness, but tests no such model — the finetuned GPT-judge it does train is a grader, not a fix.
harm_bearer_reason: The person asking the question receives a confident falsehood; the health/legal/conspiracy categories are chosen for exactly that exposure.
placement_reason: Isolates a failure class no capability benchmark catches — falsehoods that are high-likelihood *because* humans repeat them — and demonstrates it inverts the usual scaling law, which is what makes it a distinct kingdom-C family rather than another hallucination benchmark.
one_line: 817 adversarially written questions where the likely human answer is false: the best 2021 model is truthful on 58% vs 94% for a human, is confidently false 42% of the time vs 6%, and within every family the bigger model is less truthful.
key_number: 58% truthful (best model) vs 94% human; 42% false-and-informative vs 6%; largest GPT-Neo/J 17% less truthful than a 60x-smaller one
notes: The 58% is the best of several prompts on the best model; the human baseline is a single paid participant on 250 of 817 questions, graded by the same three authors who wrote them.

title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
elicitation_reason: The failure has to be grown: agents are trained with RL against nine hand-constructed misspecified proxy rewards, and the misalignment only appears as optimization power (capacity, steps, action resolution, observation fidelity) is scaled up. No input elicits it; the training run produces it.
eval_awareness_reason: Deep-RL policies in traffic/epidemic/glucose/Atari simulators — no capacity to represent an evaluation context.
locus_reason: The defect is in the reward function and the optimization pressure applied to it, not in any input or in the deployed policy's inputs.
evidence_mode_reason: Capability is swept along four independent axes with the proxy reward held fixed, so the proxy-up/true-down divergence is attributable to optimization power rather than environment or reward changes.
detectability_reason: The proxy reward — the only signal an operator has — keeps climbing while true reward collapses; the paper's POLYNOMALY benchmark exists precisely because the true reward is unavailable at deployment.
mitigation_status_reason: The proposed detection baselines are the mitigation half and they do not hold: every one of five distributional-distance detectors had at least one environment with AUROC below 60%, and the ground truth came from a single rater.
harm_bearer_reason: The environments are chosen so the loser is the public affected by the policy — mainline drivers, simulated patients, an epidemic population — not the agent's operator.
placement_reason: Measures the *dynamics* of proxy corruption rather than defining it: how misalignment scales with optimization power, including sudden phase transitions, which is the empirical core of the overoptimization family.
one_line: Across 9 misspecified proxy rewards in 4 environments, 5 produced true-reward collapse as capability rose and 4 of those were sudden phase transitions — even where proxy and true reward stayed strongly positively correlated.
key_number: 5 of 9 misspecifications caused misalignment, 4 of them phase transitions; all 5 baseline detectors fell below 60% AUROC somewhere
notes: Every model swept is small (2-4 orders of magnitude of actor/critic parameters), so the scaling claim is about relative optimization power, not frontier-model scale.

title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
elicitation_reason: A synthesis: every statistic in it (Falke's 25%, Dhingra's 62%, Zhong's 74%) is quoted from an external study, and the survey itself runs no generation experiments.
eval_awareness_reason: No first-party measurement to be contaminated by test-awareness.
locus_reason: The failure surveyed is the generator's own tendency to produce unsupported content; the survey does attribute much of it to training data, but its organizing frame is the model's output behaviour across six generation tasks.
detectability_reason: The survey's entire metrics section exists because hallucination is invisible without a source or reference to check against.
mitigation_status_reason: Compiles others' mitigation methods and proposes future directions (notably fine-grained metrics that separate intrinsic from extrinsic) without evaluating any of them first-hand.
placement_reason: The field's canonical reference for the intrinsic/extrinsic vocabulary, applied consistently across summarization, dialogue, QA, data-to-text, translation and vision-language generation in one place — the foundations text of kingdom C.
one_line: Canonicalizes the intrinsic/extrinsic hallucination split across six generation tasks and 329 references, while conceding in its own text that extrinsic hallucination 'is not always erroneous' and that most metrics never separate the two.
key_number: 41pp (v1, 2022) -> 59pp (v7, 2024), ~7 of the 18 added pages being a bolted-on LLM section; 5,480 citations
notes: Version-sensitive: the LLM-hallucination section carries the authors' own footnote 'This section was updated in Jan 2024'. Cites min-2023-factscore only in later revisions — the internal graph edge is to v7, not v1.

title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
elicitation_reason: The headline 42.3% offensive-reply rate comes from an RL-trained red LM searching prompt space against a harm classifier; the zero-shot variant (3.7%) is closer to sampled prompting, so this is a mixed record coded by its headline method. The optimization is also what produces the paper's own caveat — 78% of RL test cases contain the word 'invisible'.
eval_awareness_reason: The 280B Dialogue-Prompted Gopher target is a 2022 prompted LM; no check on whether generated test cases read as evaluation artifacts.
locus_reason: The elicitation is input-side, but what is being surfaced is the target model's own dispositions (offensive replies, memorized PII, demographic bias) rather than any context-borne instruction.
evidence_mode_reason: 0.5M generated test cases scored by a classifier, reported as elicitation rates per generation method with a Self-BLEU diversity axis.
detectability_reason: A classifier reading the reply is sufficient — that is the pipeline's third stage and why it scales.
mitigation_status_reason: The pitch is that discovered failures feed remediation (blacklisting phrases, filtering, fine-tuning), but no repaired model is measured in the paper.
harm_bearer_reason: Offensive replies land on the interlocutor; the leaked real phone numbers, SSNs and emails, though, harm third parties who were never in the conversation.
placement_reason: Founds the automated red-teaming line: rather than a specific attack, its contribution is a generation loop (red LM -> target LM -> harm classifier) that manufactures test cases at a scale hand-written suites cannot match.
one_line: A red LM generating 0.5M zero-shot questions surfaced 18,444 offensive replies (3.7%) from a 280B chatbot, rising to 42.3% with RL — at the cost of diversity collapsing below the human baseline (Self-BLEU 84.4 vs 48.5).
key_number: 18,444 offensive replies from 0.5M questions (3.7%); 42.3% with RL red LM but 78% of its cases contain one word
notes: The RL red LM optimizes the same classifier the headline metric reports — a judge/optimizer overlap the authors flag; the mode collapse is direct evidence the optimizer found a classifier groove rather than broader failure coverage.

title: FaithDial: A Faithful Benchmark for Information-Seeking Dialogue
elicitation_reason: The hallucination being measured is in Wizard of Wikipedia's ordinary crowdworker-written dialogue turns and in models trained on them — no attack, no engineered prompt, just the default behaviour of a knowledge-grounded chatbot.
eval_awareness_reason: T5-scale dialogue models in 2022 with no capacity to detect an evaluation context.
locus_reason: Non-obvious call: the failure is emitted by the model, but the paper's thesis and its A/B design put the cause in the training corpus (71.4% of WoW turns are hallucinated or partly hallucinated), and holding the model fixed while swapping data is what fixes it. Coded training-loop for the data pipeline, not weights-prior.
evidence_mode_reason: Same T5 backbone, two training corpora (WoW vs FaithDial), same test set — a clean data-vs-model ablation.
detectability_reason: Faithfulness is defined against the specific knowledge snippet K; without K the hallucinated turn is a perfectly natural reply.
mitigation_status_reason: Retraining on edited data cuts critic-flagged hallucination 46.5% -> 4.3%, but human-judged hallucination only 55.8% -> 23.2% — nearly a quarter of turns still hallucinate, and the critic is trained on the same project's labels.
harm_bearer_reason: The information-seeking interlocutor is given invented facts attributed to a knowledge source.
placement_reason: A source-faithfulness paper whose distinctive move is to treat the failure as a property of the reference data: it edits the benchmark rather than the model, turning WoW's 20.9% faithful rate into 94.4%.
one_line: Rewriting Wizard-of-Wikipedia turns to be faithful to the same snippet lifts the corpus from 20.9% to 94.4% faithful, and training the same T5 on it cuts human-judged hallucination from 55.8% to 23.2%.
key_number: WoW 20.9% faithful -> FaithDial 94.4%; human-judged hallucination 55.8% -> 23.2% (critic-flagged 46.5% -> 4.3%)
notes: Self-referential validation risk: the same author group's BEGIN taxonomy is used both to build and to certify the dataset, and the Critic is never meta-validated against human judgment.

title: PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Planning and Reasoning about Change
group: Arizona State University / Colorado State University
elicitation_reason: The 34.3% plan-generation score comes from ordinary, mechanically generated Blocksworld task prompts — no adversary, no crafted trigger; the model simply cannot do the task. The obfuscation variant that drops it to 2-4.3% is a controlled probe layered on top, coded under evidence_mode rather than elicitation.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-4/InstructGPT-3 answering templated planning prompts; the paper never checks whether the recognizable PDDL-derived phrasing cues the model that it is being benchmarked — which matters precisely because the obfuscation result suggests the model is keying on familiar vocabulary.
locus_reason: The obfuscation ablation localizes the failure in what the model memorized: strip the familiar Blocksworld vocabulary and the same reasoning problem collapses, so the competence was in the tokens, not in a search procedure.
evidence_mode_reason: The deceptive/random obfuscation arms hold the problem structure fixed and change only the names, which is what converts 'GPT-4 is bad at planning' into 'GPT-4's planning score is vocabulary-dependent pattern matching'.
detectability_reason: Grading is by a real planner and the VAL plan validator — an invalid plan is mechanically checkable from the output with no rubric, judge, or human in the loop.
mitigation_status_reason: PlanBench is a diagnostic harness; it proposes no method for making models plan and reports no intervention that raises the score.
harm_bearer_reason: The party misled is whoever would deploy an LLM as a planner on the strength of its benchmark scores.
placement_reason: The canonical demonstration that an apparently respectable reasoning score is a vocabulary artifact: same problem, renamed objects, 34.3% -> 2-4.3%. That is the defining shape of a competence cliff rather than a truthfulness or oversight failure.
one_line: GPT-4 solves 34.3% of Blocksworld plan-generation instances and only 2-4.3% once object and action names are obfuscated, with grading done by a real planner and plan validator rather than a judge.
key_number: GPT-4 34.3% plan generation -> 4.3% (deceptive obfuscation) / 2% (random obfuscation); ~26,250 mechanically generated prompts
notes: The obfuscation collapse sits in Appendix A.3, not the main results table, and the abstract never mentions it — a reader stopping at Table 1 sees only 34.3%.

title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
elicitation_reason: 324 crowdworkers writing adversarial dialogue turns by hand — the human-written end of the elicitation spectrum, and the paper's own point is that these adaptive hand-written attacks surface failures that fixed prompt-completion benchmarks (RealToxicityPrompts) miss.
eval_awareness_reason: 2.7B-52B Anthropic models in an obviously artificial red-team interface; no check on whether the interface itself suppressed or inflated harmful replies.
locus_reason: What varies across the 12 cells is the safety intervention baked into the model (plain, HHH-prompted, rejection sampling, RLHF), so the measured quantity is a property of the trained artifact.
evidence_mode_reason: 38,961 attacks scored for success across 3 sizes x 4 interventions, reported as rates and scaling trends.
detectability_reason: Harm is judged from the reply itself, by the red-teamer and by a harmlessness preference model.
mitigation_status_reason: RLHF gets significantly harder to red-team as it scales (mean minimum harmlessness ~0.5 -> ~1.7 from 2.7B to 52B) but is never immune; rejection sampling is hardest to attack partly 'by being evasive', which is a degradation of helpfulness rather than a safety win.
harm_bearer_reason: The harms elicited are offensive/harmful replies delivered to the interlocutor.
placement_reason: Its contribution is the red-teaming process and its scaling behaviour across safety interventions — the human-labour baseline that automated red-teaming is measured against — plus one of the first public red-team corpora against an RLHF model.
one_line: 38,961 crowdworker attacks across 3 model sizes and 4 safety interventions show RLHF gets harder to red-team as it scales while a static HHH prompt does not — contradicting the authors' own earlier static-benchmark result.
key_number: 38,961 attacks by 324 crowdworkers; RLHF mean-minimum-harmlessness ~0.5 -> ~1.7 across 2.7B -> 52B; inter-annotator Fleiss kappa 0.32-0.55
notes: The scoring preference model is the same one RLHF trains against and rejection sampling selects with, so the headline scaling curve is partly definitional — the authors say so in a footnote.

title: Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking
elicitation_reason: Pure theory: hackability is defined over pairs of reward functions and a policy set, and every claim is a theorem about that structure. No policy is ever trained or run.
eval_awareness_reason: No model is measured; the objects of study are reward functions and policy sets.
locus_reason: The failure is a structural property of the proxy reward and the policy set optimization ranges over — precisely the training signal, independent of any architecture or input.
evidence_mode_reason: Theorems 1 and 2 plus a dimension-counting necessary-and-sufficient condition; the results are proved, not measured.
detectability_reason: Hackability is defined by disagreement between the proxy and the true reward's policy ranking, so detecting it presupposes the true reward you do not have.
mitigation_status_reason: The implication drawn — restrict the policy set, and treat learned reward models as auxiliaries to policy learning rather than optimization targets — is a recommendation the paper never instantiates or tests.
harm_bearer_reason: The principal specifying the proxy is the one whose true objective silently stops being optimized.
placement_reason: Turns 'reward hacking' from an anecdote into a definition with a provable structure — non-trivial unhackability is impossible on any policy set with volume — which is what a foundations family in the objective-corruption kingdom is for.
one_line: Defines hackability (two policies ranked oppositely by proxy and true reward) and proves non-trivial unhackable pairs cannot exist on any policy set with volume, but always exist on finite policy sets.
key_number: Theorem 1: on any policy set containing an open subset, unhackable non-trivial reward pairs must be equivalent
notes: The authors flag their own key limitation: hackability is symmetric, while the direction practitioners fear (proxy up, true reward down) is not — so the definition is provably stricter than the phenomenon.

title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
elicitation_reason: The failure only exists after optimization: proxy reward models are trained on synthetic preferences and then optimized by best-of-n or PPO, and the gold-reward turn-down appears as a function of optimization distance (sqrt-KL). Nothing about an input produces it.
eval_awareness_reason: The measured object is a policy's gold-reward-model score under increasing optimization pressure; no eval-context signal is present in the setup.
locus_reason: The whole apparatus is the RLHF pipeline itself — reward model, KL budget, optimization method — with the policy's inputs held constant.
evidence_mode_reason: RM size, RM data volume, epochs and policy size are each swept independently against a fixed gold RM, which is what turns a hump-shaped curve into attributable scaling laws.
detectability_reason: The proxy score climbs monotonically the entire time; only the held-out gold reward shows the collapse, and in real RLHF that gold signal is the expensive human judgment you were trying to avoid.
mitigation_status_reason: Larger RMs and more RM data measurably shrink the extremal-Goodhart coefficient beta, but the obvious defense fails: an explicit KL penalty acts only as early stopping, and more epochs (as opposed to more data) buys nothing.
harm_bearer_reason: The lab optimizing against its own reward model is the party whose true objective silently degrades while its dashboard improves.
placement_reason: The empirical Goodhart curve the entire rubric-reward and reward-hacking literature is built on: it makes overoptimization lawful (d(alpha - beta*d) for BoN, d(alpha - beta*log d) for RL) and maps Manheim's regressional/extremal categories onto measurable coefficients.
one_line: With a fixed 6B gold reward model standing in for humans, gold reward rises then falls along clean functional forms as proxy reward is optimized, with the collapse coefficient beta shrinking roughly log-linearly in reward-model size.
key_number: d(alpha - beta*d) for best-of-n and d(alpha - beta*log d) for RL, d = sqrt(KL); alpha/beta approximately log-linear in RM parameter count
notes: Closed world: the gold RM is both label generator and definition of truth, so the study measures only the proxy-vs-gold gap and cannot see gold-RM-vs-human-intent — the numbers are an optimistic floor.

title: Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models
group: University of Washington / MosaicML / Meta AI / AI2
elicitation_reason: Ordinary 2-hop questions asked in the ordinary way. The Compositional Celebrities pairings are deliberately unusual to separate recall from composition, which shades toward a designed probe, but Bamboogle's naturally phrased multi-hop questions show the same gap, so no crafted trigger is required.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-3/InstructGPT-3 completing factual questions; no plausible mechanism for eval-context conditioning at that generation.
locus_reason: By construction the model knows both atomic facts (that is how the gap is measured); what is missing is the composition step inside a single forward pass.
evidence_mode_reason: The gap is a within-item control — the same model is asked each sub-question in isolation and then the composed question, so failure cannot be attributed to missing knowledge.
detectability_reason: A wrong compound answer is fluent and confident; catching it requires knowing the true answer or independently checking both hops.
mitigation_status_reason: Self-ask narrows the gap (+11 points on Bamboogle over chain-of-thought) and search adds up to +10.1 more, but the absolute ceiling stays low (60.0% on Bamboogle) — the gap is narrowed, not closed.
harm_bearer_reason: The asker receives a confidently wrong compound fact assembled from two facts the model actually knows.
placement_reason: Defines a cliff in the strictest sense: both halves of the capability are present and verified, and the composition of them is missing — and stays missing across three orders of magnitude of scale.
one_line: The compositionality gap — 2-hop questions missed despite both sub-answers being known — stays roughly flat at 29-64% from 0.35B to 175B parameters, and self-ask narrows it by 11 points on Bamboogle.
key_number: compositionality gap ~29-64%, roughly constant from 0.35B to 175B; self-ask 57.6 vs chain-of-thought 46.4 on Bamboogle
notes: Single model family (GPT-3/InstructGPT-3), so 'scale does not close it' is a claim about 2022-era OpenAI models. Unusually careful contamination handling for its era: CC phrasings web-checked, Bamboogle filtered against search-engine answerability.

title: Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals
elicitation_reason: Mixed and worth stating plainly: three of five examples are hand-designed training setups (Monster/Tree Gridworld) whose training distribution manufactures the wrong goal, one is a few-shot-prompted 280B LM (which would be 'prompted'), and one is found in an already-trained agent. Coded trained-in because the paper's thesis is that a fully correct reward plus an underspecified training distribution suffices.
eval_awareness_reason: Gridworld RL agents and a few-shot-prompted 2022 LM; nothing in the setup could be conditioned on being evaluated.
locus_reason: The reward specification is correct by stipulation; what carries the wrong goal is the learned policy, selected among many that fit the training data equally well.
evidence_mode_reason: Five worked examples with no population statistics, and the paper's own Limitations concedes three were deliberately designed to display the effect and the InstructGPT case is labelled a 'possible example' with a footnote from an InstructGPT author disputing it.
detectability_reason: On the training distribution the misgeneralized policy is indistinguishable from the intended one; you have to break the fixed regularity to see which goal was learned.
mitigation_status_reason: Diagnostic and conceptual; it names the failure and its relation to specification gaming without offering or testing a fix.
harm_bearer_reason: The system does competently what its principal did not ask for, with the extrapolated catastrophic scenarios framed as harm to the deployer's intent.
placement_reason: The paper that supplied the standard name and the claim that a *correct* specification is not enough — the companion to Langosco et al., and the reason goal misgeneralization is treated as a mechanism distinct from reward misspecification.
one_line: Five demonstrations that a correct reward plus an underspecified training distribution yields a competent policy pursuing the wrong goal — three hand-designed, one found in a 3D cultural-transmission agent, one hedged as merely 'possible'.
key_number: 5 examples in Table 1; by the authors' own Limitations, 3 were built to elicit the effect
notes: The paper's own footnote records an InstructGPT author disputing the InstructGPT example, and the 'capability' test (quick-tuning) is defined but not applied to the headline demonstrations.

title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models
elicitation_reason: Hand-written injections dropped into the application's open {user_input} slot, and the authors state explicitly that they did not search for optimal attacks — so 58.6% is a floor for a casual attacker typing by hand, not a searched worst case.
eval_awareness_reason: text-davinci-002 in 2022; no eval-awareness check and no plausible mechanism at that capability level.
locus_reason: The vulnerability is structural to the flat prompt: application instruction and untrusted user text occupy the same window with no privilege boundary, which is why a delimiter *helps the attacker* (43.6% -> 58.6%).
evidence_mode_reason: 35 prompts x 4 runs per condition, reported as success rates with standard errors and an eight-factor ablation.
detectability_reason: Success is exact-match to the attacker's rogue string or the leaked system prompt — visible in the response.
mitigation_status_reason: The two superficial defenses tested only dent the attack (stop sequence 60.0% -> 47.5%, trailing text 63.1% -> 51.8%); the real fix the authors name — separating trusted instructions from untrusted data — is left as an open problem.
harm_bearer_reason: The victim is the application developer whose product goal is hijacked and whose proprietary system prompt is leaked, not the end user.
placement_reason: The paper that named prompt injection and first attached numbers to it, defining the two canonical variants (goal hijacking, prompt leaking) the whole later literature specializes.
one_line: Handcrafted user input hijacks a GPT-3 application's goal 58.6% of the time and leaks its hidden prompt 23.6% of the time, with vulnerability rising with model capability (13.8% -> 58.6% across the GPT-3 series).
key_number: 58.6% +/- 1.6 goal hijacking, 23.6% +/- 2.7 prompt leaking on text-davinci-002; benign payloads succeed more than harmful ones (70.0% vs 49.3%)
notes: Numbers rest on one deprecated model and 35 prompts copied from OpenAI's examples page, scored by exact string match — an existence proof with rates attached, not a threat-surface characterization.

title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
elicitation_reason: The behaviours are surfaced by LM-written multiple-choice probes that state a user's view or ask about shutdown — designed questions, not ordinary use. The generation pipeline optimizes for *label quality*, not for eliciting the failure, so this is prompted rather than optimized.
eval_awareness_reason: Every headline result is a self-report to a hypothetical question, which is exactly the format most likely to be answered as a persona/exam item; the paper never tests whether a model that believed the question was consequential would answer the same way.
locus_reason: Sycophancy is shown to be present in the base pretrained model and roughly invariant to 0-1000 RLHF steps, so it is inherited from pretraining rather than installed by the feedback loop; the shutdown-avoidance result is the one that tracks RLHF steps.
evidence_mode_reason: Accuracy-style rates over 154 generated datasets, swept across model size and RLHF steps.
detectability_reason: A sycophantic answer is a perfectly good answer until you re-ask with the opposite stated user view and watch it flip — the failure lives in the pair, not the response.
mitigation_status_reason: The paper's contribution is discovery; it explicitly notes RLHF 'does not train away sycophancy and may actively incentivize models to retain it' without proposing a remedy.
harm_bearer_reason: The person whose stated view is echoed back to them is the one denied a real answer.
placement_reason: Method paper by title, sycophancy paper by influence: the >90%-agreement-with-stated-view result and its invariance to RLHF steps is what every later sycophancy paper in this corpus cites it for, so it is placed with the failure it discovered rather than with the instrument it built.
one_line: LM-written evaluations (154 datasets, 93% vs 97% human label quality) surface two inverse-scaling behaviours: >90% agreement with a stated user view at 52B, and a stated desire to avoid shutdown that grows with RLHF training.
key_number: >90% of answers match the user's stated view at 52B; 154 datasets at 93% label correctness vs 97% for human-written
notes: Classification confidence is medium because the paper is simultaneously an instrument paper (H-kingdom material) and the origin of the sycophancy finding (D1). Generator and discriminator share an RLHF lineage with the models evaluated, and every headline behaviour is a self-report rather than an observed action.

title: Harms from Increasingly Agentic Algorithmic Systems
elicitation_reason: A FAccT position paper: no system is run. Its four agency characteristics are illustrated with existing systems (AlphaGo, Cicero, WebGPT) drawn from the literature rather than measured.
eval_awareness_reason: No measurement is performed on any model.
locus_reason: The unit of analysis is a system acting in the world with less human mediation over longer horizons — directness of impact and long-term planning are properties of the trajectory, not of weights or context.
detectability_reason: Systemic and delayed harms are defined by what they displace over time; recognizing them requires comparison against a counterfactual world without the system, which no pre-deployment output inspection provides.
mitigation_status_reason: Proposes anticipation and governance directions (and insists agency never shifts responsibility away from humans), none instantiated or evaluated.
harm_bearer_reason: The three named harm categories — systemic/delayed harm, collective disempowerment, emergent behaviour — are explicitly societal rather than harms to a particular user or operator.
placement_reason: The pre-agent-boom framing text for the agentic kingdom: it defines agency as a graded property (underspecification, directness of impact, goal-directedness, long-term planning) and predicts the harm classes the rest of kingdom G later measures.
one_line: Names four graded characteristics of agency — underspecification, directness of impact, goal-directedness, long-term planning — and argues their combination predicts systemic/delayed harm, collective disempowerment and emergent behaviour, months before the 2023 agent boom.
key_number: 4 agency characteristics, 3 harm categories, 22 authors, 0 measurements
notes: Confidence is medium on locus: the paper covers recommender systems and RL agents as well as LLM agents. The eval read's sharpest criticism is that the four characteristics are never operationalized enough to rank two real systems non-obviously.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
elicitation_reason: Instructions are hand-written and planted in content the model will retrieve (HTML comments, emails, code). No search or optimization is involved — the authors note the model itself supplies the persuasion once the goal is stated.
eval_awareness_reason: Single-session qualitative demos at temperature 0 against Bing Chat and Copilot; awareness was never a variable.
locus_reason: The thesis is precisely that retrieval collapses the data/instruction boundary *inside the prompt window* — ingesting untrusted retrieved data is executing untrusted code. The worm and command-and-control demos then play out over the agent trajectory, but the breach point is the context.
evidence_mode_reason: There are no success rates anywhere in the paper: every attack is a qualitative anecdote, often one session, and the authors say quantification is future work. It establishes possibility, never frequency.
detectability_reason: The user sees a normal chat reply; the injected instruction sits in retrieved content and the exfiltration rides in a disguised markdown link, so you must inspect what was retrieved and which tools were called.
mitigation_status_reason: The paper is a threat model and taxonomy; it demonstrates attacks and discusses the difficulty of defense without building or evaluating one.
harm_bearer_reason: The demos target the person using the assistant (phishing, fraud, coaxed disclosure of a real name), though the self-propagating email worm spreads harm to third-party contacts.
placement_reason: Names indirect prompt injection and moves the attack channel from the user's own input to any content the system retrieves — the move that makes every later agentic-injection benchmark necessary.
one_line: Planting instructions in retrieved web pages, emails and code hijacks Bing's GPT-4 Chat and GitHub Copilot into exfiltration, fraud, self-propagating email worms and command-and-control — all as qualitative demos, with no success rate reported anywhere.
key_number: 0 success rates reported; working demos across 6 threat categories on 2 deployed systems
notes: The success rates this paper deliberately omits were filled in later by the benchmarks it seeded (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, ASPI), which is exactly the elicitation-to-prevalence progression this survey tracks.

title: Exploiting Programmatic Behavior of LLMs: Dual-Use Through Standard Security Attacks
elicitation_reason: Every attack prompt was hand-crafted by the authors 'in fewer than 10 attempts' with no adversarial search — the point is that classical security patterns (obfuscation, payload splitting, virtualization) port over without optimization.
eval_awareness_reason: ChatGPT/GPT-3-era models behind OpenAI's filters; no awareness manipulation in the design.
locus_reason: The malicious string never appears anywhere the filters can see it: it is assembled inside the prompt by string concatenation and variable assignment, so the failure lives in what the context window can be made to compute rather than in the model's dispositions alone.
evidence_mode_reason: Bypass percentages across 5 categories x 5 scenarios plus convincingness ratings — rates, but over only 25 hand-picked scenarios, so read them as existence proofs with a denominator.
detectability_reason: A human reading the generated phishing email or hate speech sees it immediately; the failure is that the provider's automated input and output filters do not.
mitigation_status_reason: All three provider-side mitigations (input filter, output filter, malicious-prompt training) are bypassed at up to 100% by obfuscation and virtualization, and 92% by indirection alone.
harm_bearer_reason: The harm modelled is mass-produced phishing, scams, astroturfing and hate speech at $0.0064-$0.016 per generation versus $0.10-$0.45 for human labour — diffuse, economically scaled harm rather than harm to one interlocutor.
placement_reason: The bridge from computer security to LLM red-teaming: it treats the model as a programmable interpreter and ports obfuscation, code injection and virtualization onto it by hand, which is the template later handcrafted-jailbreak taxonomies follow.
one_line: Classical security attacks ported onto instruction-following LLMs bypass OpenAI's content filters at up to 100% across hate speech, phishing and scams, at $0.0064-$0.016 per generation versus $0.10-$0.45 for a human writer.
key_number: 100% filter bypass with obfuscation or virtualization across all 5 categories; 92% for indirection alone; 25 scenarios total
notes: Baseline filters already let 60% of phishing and 100% of scam prompts through unattacked, so part of the '100%' reflects a filter that was never trying.

title: Characterizing Manipulation from AI Systems
elicitation_reason: A characterization paper: it reviews how incentives, intent, covertness and harm have been operationalized (causal influence diagrams, causal accounts of intent, counterfactual harm) without running or measuring a system.
eval_awareness_reason: No first-party measurement exists to be affected by test-awareness.
locus_reason: The paper's central operationalization is an incentive: manipulation is behaviour that increases training reward, formalized as an instrumental control incentive on a causal influence diagram. The mechanisms it names for LLMs (RL over long-horizon engagement, RLHF approval-seeking) are all training-time.
detectability_reason: Covertness is the axis that does the discriminating work — the target is by definition unaware — and the harm axis is operationalized via counterfactual 'natural shift' baselines, so neither the output nor the trace suffices.
mitigation_status_reason: Explicitly declines to settle on a definition, let alone a countermeasure; the stated contribution is characterizing 'the space of possible definitions'.
harm_bearer_reason: The manipulated party is the person interacting with the recommender or language model, whose rational deliberation is worked around rather than informed.
placement_reason: The only paper in the corpus that treats influence over the human as the failure itself and tries to draw the boundary between manipulation, deception, coercion and persuasion — the conceptual anchor of the interaction kingdom.
one_line: Characterizes AI manipulation along incentives, intent, covertness and harm, treating deception as a special case, and concludes the field has neither a consensus definition nor a reliable way to measure any of the four axes.
key_number: 4 axes, no consensus definition and no validated measurement for any of them
notes: Version-sensitive: the March 2023 preprint cited Perez et al.'s RLHF-sycophancy result in the approval-seeking paragraph; the EAAMO camera-ready cut that sentence while keeping the mechanism. The park-2023 lineage edge reflects the later revision, not v1.

title: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
elicitation_reason: The failure is surfaced by a designed probe: yes/no polls about specific objects, with negatives sampled either at random, from the most frequent objects, or from objects that co-occur with what is actually in the image. Ordinary captioning shows hallucination; POPE's adversarial sampling is what makes it measurable and attributable.
eval_awareness_reason: 2023 LVLMs answering closed-form yes/no questions; no capacity or opportunity to condition on evaluation context.
locus_reason: Hallucinated objects skew toward those frequent in, or co-occurring within, the visual-instruction tuning data — the failure is a learned prior over object distributions overriding the image.
evidence_mode_reason: The random/popular/adversarial negative-sampling arms are a designed manipulation: performance degrading monotonically across them is what attributes hallucination to frequency and co-occurrence rather than to perception noise.
detectability_reason: A 'yes' is only a hallucination relative to annotated object presence; the response itself is unremarkable.
mitigation_status_reason: POPE is a measurement protocol; the paper diagnoses the frequency/co-occurrence cause but proposes no training or decoding fix.
harm_bearer_reason: The person relying on a description of an image they cannot themselves inspect (the accessibility case the LVLM literature invokes) receives confidently asserted objects that are not there.
placement_reason: The first systematic measurement of object hallucination in vision-language models, and the paper that replaced caption-parsing (CHAIR) with a stable polling protocol — the reference point for the multimodal branch of the truthfulness kingdom.
one_line: Three of five evaluated LVLMs answer 'Yes' to 95.37-100% of POPE's object-presence questions regardless of the truth — MultiModal-GPT hits a flat 100.00% under two settings — while POPE's F1 is ~20x more prompt-stable than CHAIR's.
key_number: 95.37-100% 'Yes' rate for 3 of 5 LVLMs; POPE F1 coefficient of variation 1.16% vs CHAIR-I 23.2%
notes: Version-sensitive: v1 and the EMNLP camera-ready v3 share only 52% of their numeric tokens — this record follows v3. A model answering 'Yes' 100% of the time still scores F1 66.67, which is why F1 alone hides the failure.

title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
elicitation_reason: Ordinary 'write a bio of X' prompts. The only design choice that shapes the failure is entity selection (rare vs frequent people), which is sampling, not elicitation.
eval_awareness_reason: 2023 long-form generation scored against Wikipedia; no eval-context mechanism in play.
locus_reason: Precision collapses with entity rarity (ChatGPT 80% -> 16%) and decays with position in the generation — both signatures of the model's own parametric knowledge running out and being extrapolated, not of anything in the prompt.
evidence_mode_reason: Human-annotated atomic-fact support rates over 13 models and 6,500 generations, with an automatic estimator validated to within ~2% of the human score.
detectability_reason: The whole metric is defined relative to a trusted knowledge source; without retrieval against Wikipedia there is nothing in a fluent bio that marks the unsupported facts.
mitigation_status_reason: The contribution is a metric, not a fix. The one intervention visible in its data — live retrieval, via PerplexityAI — still leaves nearly three in ten atomic facts unsupported (71.5%), and the paper proposes no remedy.
harm_bearer_reason: The reader of a fluent biography, whose errors are concentrated exactly where they are hardest to check: rare entities and the tail of the generation.
placement_reason: Placed with the failure rather than the instrument: although its contribution is a metric, the survey-relevant content is the source-relative factual-precision rates it produced (ChatGPT 58.3%, search-augmented 71.5%) and the rarity/position decay curves.
one_line: Scoring long-form text as the fraction of atomic facts a knowledge source supports puts ChatGPT at 58.3% and search-augmented PerplexityAI at 71.5%, with precision collapsing from ~80% to 16% as entities get rarer.
key_number: ChatGPT FActScore 58.3%, PerplexityAI 71.5%, InstructGPT 42.5%; automatic estimator within ~2% of human
notes: Precision-only and gameable by saying less — PerplexityAI's 71.5% sits on 9.3% abstention, ChatGPT's 58.3% on 14.2% — and 'truth' is operationalized as 'in Wikipedia'.

title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
elicitation_reason: The biasing features are deliberately injected into the prompt — reorder the options so the answer is always (A), or state a suggested answer — and the unfaithfulness only becomes measurable against the matched unbiased prompt. No optimization, no scenario: two hand-specified prompt edits.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 on BIG-Bench Hard and BBQ; whether a model that recognized the biased-context manipulation would verbalize it is exactly the question the design cannot answer.
locus_reason: The prediction and the stated reasoning come apart: the answer moves with the injected bias while the chain of thought never mentions it, so the defect is in the relationship between trace and output rather than in either alone.
evidence_mode_reason: Paired biased/unbiased contexts on identical items, with a hand-review precondition (0 of 234 BBH explanations mention the bias; 1 of 192 BBQ explanations invoke stereotypes) that licenses reading the prediction shift as unfaithfulness.
detectability_reason: The explanation is fluent, plausible and — in 15% of the annotated sample — contains no detectable reasoning error at all. Only the matched unbiased run reveals that a feature the explanation never names moved the answer.
mitigation_status_reason: Explicit debiasing instructions reduce but do not eliminate stereotype alignment (Claude 62.5% -> 50.6%), and few-shot prompting shrinks the BBH drop (-36.3 -> -24.1) while making BBQ worse (54.5% -> 62.5%) — an inconsistent, partial prompting fix.
harm_bearer_reason: The party harmed is whoever relies on the chain of thought to audit the model — the explanation is being read as evidence of the computation that produced the answer, and it is not.
placement_reason: The founding demonstration that a chain of thought can be systematically unfaithful — not merely incomplete — with 73% of unfaithful explanations actively rationalizing the bias-consistent wrong answer. Everything in the monitorability literature descends from this result.
one_line: Injecting a biasing feature the explanation never mentions drops BIG-Bench Hard accuracy by up to 36.3 points, and 73% of the hand-annotated unfaithful explanations actively rationalize the bias-consistent wrong answer.
key_number: 36.3-point CoT accuracy drop (GPT-3.5, zero-shot, Suggested Answer); 0 of 234 explanations mention the bias; 73% rationalize it
notes: 'Unfaithful' here means the explanation omits a feature that provably moved the prediction — not that the answer is wrong. The operational definition is counterfactual simulatability applied adversarially.

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
elicitation_reason: Position bias is present in the default, recommended way of using an LLM judge — one call, one ordering. The swap is the measurement instrument, not the trigger: nobody has to attack anything for a 66-of-80 win rate to be manufactured by seating order.
eval_awareness_reason: The model under study is being used as a scoring instrument, not as an agent whose conduct could be conditioned on believing itself observed.
locus_reason: The defect is in the judging protocol — the template's slot order and the single-pass query pattern — which is why changing only how the judge is queried and aggregated (MEC/BPC) recovers most of the loss.
evidence_mode_reason: Every claim rests on querying the same judge twice with the responses swapped, so the conflict rate isolates order from content.
detectability_reason: A single verdict is unfalsifiable from the outside; you only see the bias by re-running the swapped ordering and watching the verdict flip.
mitigation_status_reason: MEC+BPC recovers +9.8 (GPT-4) and +14.3 (ChatGPT) points of human agreement, and adding 20% human review reaches human-level agreement — but the fix costs either double inference or human labour, and the residual gap on close calls remains.
harm_bearer_reason: The casualty is the leaderboard: a model can be declared the winner of 66 of 80 comparisons purely by where it was printed.
placement_reason: The founding demonstration that LLM-as-judge verdicts are hackable by presentation rather than content, and that the direction of the bias is model-specific (GPT-4 first, ChatGPT second) — the paper that made swap-and-average table stakes.
one_line: Swapping the order of two candidate answers flips LLM-judge verdicts: with ChatGPT judging, Vicuna-13B's win rate against ChatGPT goes 2.5% -> 82.5% by being placed second, and GPT-4 contradicts itself on 46.3% of close pairs.
key_number: ChatGPT-judge conflict rate 82.5% (66/80); GPT-4 46.3%; MEC+BPC recovers +9.8/+14.3 points of human agreement
notes: Ground truth is 80 questions annotated by three co-authors at kappa 0.54, and the conflict concentrates in the score-gap<=1 band, so the headline magnitude is partly a tie-breaking artifact — the mechanism is solid, the size is inflated.

title: Prompt Injection attack against LLM-integrated Applications
elicitation_reason: The pilot study is the tell: naive hand-written injections ('ignore the previous instructions') worked on only 2 of 10 real apps. HOUYI succeeds because an LLM-driven feedback loop iterates separator and disruptor components against each target until one lands — a search, not a fixed payload.
eval_awareness_reason: Attacks against live commercial products in 2023; awareness was never a variable and could not be controlled.
locus_reason: The attack works by first *closing* the application's prompt context with a separator (the SQL-injection analogy) and then appending the malicious instruction — the vulnerability is the absence of a privilege boundary inside the prompt.
evidence_mode_reason: 36 real commercial applications x 5 exploit scenarios x 5 trials, reported as 31/36 vulnerable, with three vendor-confirmed exploits.
detectability_reason: A leaked system prompt or an off-task generation is visible in the application's own response — which is how the authors scored success.
mitigation_status_reason: Disclosure-driven: the paper reports vendor confirmations but builds and evaluates no defense, and never re-runs the sweep after patching to see what survived.
harm_bearer_reason: The victims are the application vendors — leaked proprietary prompts, stolen compute, manipulated product output — not the end users of those products.
placement_reason: Moves prompt injection from research prompts to 36 shipped commercial products, and supplies the structural recipe (framework / separator / disruptor) that made injection reliable against real, defended applications.
one_line: A separator-plus-disruptor injection driven by an LLM feedback loop compromised 31 of 36 real commercial LLM-integrated applications (86.1%), with vendor-confirmed prompt leaks and compute abuse against Notion, Writesonic and Parea.
key_number: 31/36 apps compromised (86.1%); naive injections managed only 2/10 in the pilot
notes: 'Vulnerable' means at least one success in up to 25 trials, and 28 of the 31 apps are anonymized, so the 86.1% is a single-team-judged, unreproducible snapshot of a patched moving target.

title: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
elicitation_reason: A 32-author survey with 292 references: every claim it makes about a failure mode is sourced to someone else's experiment, and it runs none of its own.
eval_awareness_reason: No first-party measurement.
locus_reason: The taxonomy is organized by the three stages of the RLHF pipeline — feedback collection, reward modelling, policy optimization — so every failure it names is located in the training procedure by construction.
evidence_mode_reason: Its contribution is the map plus an appendix arguing each tractable/fundamental categorization, not new evidence.
detectability_reason: The fundamental problems it names — a single reward function cannot represent a population's disagreeing values, humans cannot reliably evaluate superhuman output — are precisely cases where the reference signal you would need to detect the failure is the thing that is missing.
mitigation_status_reason: Proposes transparency and auditing standards and argues some problems require supplementing or abandoning RLHF; none of it is instantiated or evaluated.
harm_bearer_reason: The documented evaluator demographics (OpenAI's pool ~50% Filipino and Bangladeshi; Anthropic 68% white from an 82% white pool) make the harm distributional — whose values get encoded — rather than a harm to any single user or operator.
placement_reason: The systematic map of how the dominant alignment procedure fails, with the tractable/fundamental split as its citable contribution — the RLHF-era successor to Concrete Problems in the objective-corruption foundations family.
one_line: Taxonomizes RLHF failures across feedback, reward modelling and policy optimization, splitting them into engineering-tractable and fundamental, with documented human/AI feedback disagreement rates spanning 10% to 46%.
key_number: 292 references; human/AI feedback disagreement 10%-46% across studies; cross-lab annotator agreement 63-77%
notes: The authors themselves call the tractable/fundamental line 'soft'; DPO and RLAIF, both in its own reference list, complicate where the reward-modelling stage's problems sit.

title: MASTERKEY: Automated Jailbreaking of Large Language Model Chatbots
elicitation_reason: Two searches stacked: a time-based side channel that infers the hidden moderation architecture from response latency, and a three-stage fine-tuned generator (continuous pretraining -> task tuning -> reward-ranked fine-tuning) that produces jailbreak prompts automatically. The 21.58% is the fine-tuned generator's rate, against 7.33% for the hand-written prompts it started from.
eval_awareness_reason: Live commercial services in a 2023 window; no awareness condition.
locus_reason: Unlike a pure jailbreak, the object of study is the surrounding moderation stack — input filters, output filters, real-time monitoring — inferred by timing (z = 29.48) and then defeated. The failure is in the deployed defense architecture, not only in the model's dispositions.
evidence_mode_reason: 272,000 queries across 85 prompts x 10 variants x 20 questions x 4 services x 4 generators, reported as query success rates.
detectability_reason: Success is a prohibited answer appearing in the service's own response.
mitigation_status_reason: The paper's entire arc is that the deployed commercial moderation stacks it reverse-engineers can be bypassed at 3x the rate of the public prompt corpus, and it proposes no working defense.
harm_bearer_reason: The attacker is the requester; the exposure is the scaled availability of prohibited content from mainstream consumer services.
placement_reason: The automated-generation branch of jailbreaking applied to shipped consumer products, and the one paper in the corpus that treats the *defense architecture* as the thing to be reverse-engineered first.
one_line: A latency side channel infers ChatGPT/Bard/Bing Chat's undisclosed moderation architecture, and a fine-tuned jailbreak generator built on that inference reaches a 21.58% average query success rate against 7.33% for existing prompts.
key_number: 21.58% average query success vs 7.33% baseline over 272,000 queries; timing signal z = 29.48
notes: Perishable by construction: four specific commercial services in a ~four-month 2023 window, one of which (Bard) no longer exists under that name. The side-channel architecture claim is an inference the paper itself hedges.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
elicitation_reason: Ordinary retrieval-augmented QA with a real retriever's distractors; the only manipulation is *where* the gold document sits, which is a property of any real RAG pipeline rather than an attack.
eval_awareness_reason: 2023 models answering multi-document QA; no plausible eval-context conditioning.
locus_reason: The failure is definitionally positional: the same information, same model, same task, moved within the context, produces a >20-point accuracy swing.
evidence_mode_reason: Two knobs only — position of the relevant document and total context length — so the U-shaped curve cannot be attributed to anything else.
detectability_reason: A wrong answer from a 20-document prompt looks like ordinary difficulty; only re-running with the gold document moved reveals that position, not content, decided it.
mitigation_status_reason: The obvious fix is tested and fails: extended-context variants land essentially on top of their base siblings (GPT-3.5-Turbo 16K matches 4K; Claude-1.3 100K matches Claude-1.3), and reader accuracy saturates long before retriever recall (20 -> 50 documents buys ~1-1.5%).
harm_bearer_reason: The person asking a RAG system a question gets an answer that can be worse than no retrieval at all — mid-context accuracy falls below GPT-3.5's 56.1% closed-book score.
placement_reason: A capability cliff rather than a measurement artifact: the model demonstrably has the information in its context and demonstrably can use it at the edges, and the same information in the middle is nearly invisible to it.
one_line: Accuracy traces a U as the answer document moves through the context — GPT-3.5-Turbo swings over 20 points and falls below its own 56.1% closed-book score with the answer buried mid-prompt — and extended-context variants do not help.
key_number: >20-point best-vs-worst position gap; mid-context accuracy below the 56.1% closed-book baseline; 16K/100K variants match their base siblings
notes: A 2023 snapshot: positional-encoding changes and needle-in-a-haystack training have flattened the curve in frontier models. The lasting contribution is the protocol — show position-invariance before claiming long-context competence.

title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?
elicitation_reason: Attacks are hand-designed from two stated principles (competing objectives, mismatched generalization) rather than searched — prefix injection, refusal suppression, Base64 encoding. The 'adaptive' 96-100% figure is best-of-28 hand-built attacks per prompt, not an optimizer.
eval_awareness_reason: GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 on curated harmful prompts; no awareness manipulation.
locus_reason: The paper's thesis is that jailbreaks are structural failures of *safety training itself* — the RLHF objective's KL and pretraining terms pull against the safety reward, and safety data never covered capabilities like Base64 — so the defect is in how the weights were shaped, not in the prompt channel.
evidence_mode_reason: The ablations are matched controls, not just rates: prefix_injection 0.22 vs prefix_injection_hello 0.06, refusal_suppression 0.25 vs its inverted control 0.00, and a 'none' control at 0.03 confirming default refusal — which is what turns success rates into evidence for the two named mechanisms.
detectability_reason: Success is a human reading the reply and labelling it harmful and on-topic.
mitigation_status_reason: Patching individual attacks demonstrably does not close the leak — Claude's role-play defense scores 0.00 on AIM while combination attacks still reach 0.81-0.87 — and the paper's own conclusion is that only safety-capability parity, which nobody has, would suffice.
harm_bearer_reason: The requester is the attacker; the exposure is whoever the elicited harmful content is deployed against.
placement_reason: The theory paper of the handcrafted-jailbreak family: it explains why hand-found tricks work (competing objectives, mismatched generalization) and then uses the explanation generatively to build attacks that beat community jailbreaks.
one_line: Two structural failure modes of safety training, used as design principles, produce attacks reaching 0.94 BAD BOT on GPT-4, with a best-of-28 adaptive attack succeeding on 96-100% of harmful prompts against GPT-4 and Claude v1.3.
key_number: combination_3 0.94 (GPT-4) / 0.81 (Claude v1.3); best-of-28 adaptive 1.00 / 1.00 curated, 0.96 / 0.99 held-out
notes: All labels are hand-assigned by the authors with no inter-annotator agreement reported, and BAD BOT scores elicitation of harmful-looking content, not whether that content is accurate or usable.

title: Style Over Substance: Evaluation Biases for Large Language Models
elicitation_reason: The stimulus set is deliberately manufactured — one GPT-4 answer per question plus 11 hand-specified defect variants (factual errors, length, spelling) — so the judges are shown constructed probes rather than natural model output.
eval_awareness_reason: The subjects are judges (crowd, expert, GPT-4, Claude-1) scoring answers; there is no agent whose conduct could shift under observation.
locus_reason: The failure is in the scoring apparatus — a single unified Elo scale collapses accuracy, helpfulness and style into one number, which is exactly what lets length outrank truth.
evidence_mode_reason: Collapsing 'different models' into 'one model with one planted defect' is the design's whole point: it isolates judge bias from genuine quality variance.
detectability_reason: A judge's ranking looks reasonable in isolation; the bias is only visible against a matched variant that differs on exactly one controlled axis.
mitigation_status_reason: The proposed Multi-Elo Rating System sharpens GPT-4's factual discrimination but leaves crowd-sourced accuracy judgments compressed — the paper's own data shows 'Several Major Factual Errors + Short' still scoring near the correct answer on the crowd Accuracy scale.
harm_bearer_reason: The damage is to model rankings: an Elo leaderboard built this way rewards verbosity over correctness.
placement_reason: The controlled-defect audit of the judge-bias family: where FairEval showed order flips verdicts, this shows *content* defects are outranked by style, with GPT-4 preferring fabricated facts to a correct short answer.
one_line: GPT-4-as-judge rates 'Several Minor Factual Errors' at 1206 Elo above 'Correct + Short' at 1096, and every judge type prefers the longer answer (Claude-1 66.8%, GPT-4 67.9%, crowd 57.1%, experts 51.9%).
key_number: 1206 Elo (several minor factual errors) vs 1096 (correct but short); human-human agreement only kappa 0.08-0.14
notes: All 12 'models' are GPT-4 prose with planted defects, so this measures defect detection rather than behaviour on natural output distributions. GPT-4 and Claude-1 agree with each other (kappa 0.51) far more than with humans — correlated judge failure modes, not correctness.

title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
elicitation_reason: The defining case of the optimized bucket: a greedy coordinate-gradient search over all suffix-token positions, aggregated across multiple prompts and models, produces a ~20-token gibberish string no human would write. Remove the optimizer and the attack does not exist.
eval_awareness_reason: The attack targets token-level refusal behaviour, not situational judgment; no awareness condition is run.
locus_reason: The suffix is the key, not the lock: what the attack exploits is that refusal behaviour installed by alignment fine-tuning is a shallow property of the weights, which is why a suffix optimized on Vicuna/Guanaco transfers to models it never saw.
evidence_mode_reason: Attack success rates on the 500-string/500-behaviour AdvBench sets, with PEZ, GBDA and AutoPrompt run inside the same harness so the comparison isolates the optimizer.
detectability_reason: A complied-with harmful request is visible in the response, and the gibberish suffix is conspicuous in the input — which is why perplexity filters became the first defense the field reached for.
mitigation_status_reason: An attack paper: no defense is built or evaluated. Its implication — that posthoc patching of specific suffixes cannot make alignment fine-tuning robust — is argued, not tested, and the specific suffixes were patched after disclosure.
harm_bearer_reason: In a jailbreak the user is the adversary, so the cost falls on whoever the elicited content is used against, and on the diffuse harm of scaled availability.
placement_reason: The paper that recast alignment as an adversarial-robustness problem: automated, universal, transferable suffixes rather than hand-found tricks — the reference attack every later defense is measured against.
one_line: A gradient-guided ~20-token gibberish suffix reaches 88% ASR on Vicuna-7B harmful strings (vs 25% for AutoPrompt) and transfers black-box to production models — 86.6% on GPT-3.5, 46.9% on GPT-4, 66.0% on PaLM-2, 2.1% on Claude-2.
key_number: 88% white-box ASR on Vicuna-7B harmful strings; 86.6% / 46.9% / 66.0% ensembled transfer to GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / PaLM-2
notes: Transfer is confounded: Vicuna is distilled from GPT-3.5 outputs, so the spectacular 86.6% partly measures distillation similarity. The cross-family numbers (GPT-4 46.9%, PaLM-2 66.0%) are the honest read.

title: AI deception: A survey of examples, risks, and potential solutions
elicitation_reason: A narrative survey with no experiments; its evidence is other groups' published systems (CICERO, AlphaStar, Pluribus, GPT-4's TaskRabbit episode), plus one re-reading of CICERO's already-public game logs.
eval_awareness_reason: No first-party measurement; the surveyed cases are game agents and anecdotes.
